passage:
Care home volunteer log, March. Bhupen, duty supervisor.
Tejas, 25, comes every Thursday after work. He doesn't touch anyone's feet or bow; that isn't done in his family. What he does is sit. Last week he spent an hour with Mr. D'Souza sorting old football photos, asking names and writing them on the back. He has learnt enough Assamese from Mrs. Baruah to ask about her village. He brings Mr. Hussain's newspaper folded to the crossword. Today Mrs. Baruah told me, 'That boy respects me more than my own nephews who bow and leave.' I've asked Tejas to show our new volunteers how he spends a visit.

qa.q: What did Tejas and Mr. D'Souza sort?
qa.a: Old football photos.

qa.q: What does Mrs. Baruah's comment suggest she feels about Tejas?
qa.a: It suggests she feels deep gratitude and admiration for him, valuing his time and interest more than formal bowing.

qa.q: What makes Tejas's way of honouring the residents work across different faiths and backgrounds?
qa.a: He shows respect through actions anyone understands: his time, learning their language, remembering their habits and listening.

qa.q: How might the new volunteers see respect differently after watching Tejas?
qa.a: They may realise respect can be shown through time, listening and small acts of care, without needing a particular custom like bowing.

grounding: Shows a young adult who honours elders through time, care and listening rather than the feet-touching custom, and whose respect is understood across faiths and backgrounds.

passage:
Saturday
At home I'd touch an elder's feet without thinking. Here in Toronto nobody does that, and when I first met Mrs. Kowalski downstairs, eighty-three, I just stood there awkwardly. Kalyani said, 'Just be nice, yaar.' So I've been trying. I carry her groceries up on Wednesdays. I sit with her while she tells me about her husband's bakery in Kraków. Today she taught me to make pierogi and laughed when mine burst. As I left, she squeezed my hand and said, 'You are a good girl to spend your Saturday with an old woman.' It felt like the blessing Nani gives when I touch her feet. Same thing, different language.
Mahima

qa.q: What did Mrs. Kowalski teach Mahima to make?
qa.a: Pierogi.

qa.q: What did Mahima feel when Mrs. Kowalski squeezed her hand?
qa.a: Mahima felt warm and moved, as if receiving the same blessing Nani gives.

qa.q: How did Mahima find a way to honour an elder without the feet-touching custom?
qa.a: By giving time and care: carrying groceries, listening to stories and cooking together, which anyone can understand as respect.

qa.q: What might the Saturday visits mean to Mrs. Kowalski?
qa.a: They likely ease her loneliness and make her feel valued, since she said it was good of Mahima to spend a Saturday with her.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who honours an elder through care, time and listening in a place where touching feet is not practised, and finds the respect understood across cultures.

passage:
In her first month at the school in a village near Shillong, Neelam kept reaching to touch elders' feet out of habit, and the elders kept stepping back, puzzled. Here people shook hands, or just smiled.

"You're making Kong Mary nervous," laughed Charu, the other teacher from outside the state.

So Neelam changed how she showed it. She learned to say "Khublei" properly. She sat on Kong Mary's porch every Friday while the old woman sorted betel leaves, and asked about the village before the road came. She carried the school's leftover rice to the widow at the end of the lane.

By winter, Kong Mary was introducing her to visitors: "This one listens. She is like our own."

qa.q: What does Kong Mary sort on Fridays?
qa.a: Kong Mary sorts betel leaves while Neelam sits on the porch every Friday.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when the elders kept stepping back?
qa.a: She likely felt awkward and unsure, since her usual way of showing respect confused people here.

qa.q: Which change let Neelam's respect be understood?
qa.a: Learning Khublei, sitting and listening on Kong Mary's porch every Friday and helping a neighbour; respect shown in time and care needs no gesture.

qa.q: How does Kong Mary see Neelam by winter?
qa.a: Kong Mary sees her as someone who listens and is like their own, and proudly introduces her to visitors.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a community without the feet-touching custom learning to honour elders through time, care and listening.

passage:
In Siddiq's building in Warsaw nobody touched anybody's feet, and at first he didn't know what to do with his respect.

His neighbour Marek, a retired tram driver of seventy-nine, lived alone across the landing. Siddiq started small: clearing the snow from Marek's doorstep before work, fixing the dripping tap with his own wrench. On Sundays Marek set up the chessboard and told stories about driving the number 13 through the old town, the same stories twice, sometimes three times. Siddiq listened to every one.

In March, Marek's daughter visited from Gdansk and found Siddiq there. "He calls you his boy," she said, a little surprised.

Marek grunted and moved his rook. "He listens. Nobody listens anymore."

qa.q: What was Marek's job before he retired?
qa.a: Marek was a retired tram driver.

qa.q: What does Siddiq's listening to the same stories again suggest about how he feels toward Marek?
qa.a: It suggests genuine fondness and respect; Siddiq cares more about Marek feeling heard than about being entertained.

qa.q: How does Siddiq show respect without the custom he grew up with?
qa.a: Through steady care and time: clearing snow, fixing the tap, playing chess and listening on Sundays.

qa.q: How might Marek's daughter feel finding Siddiq there?
qa.a: She is a little surprised, and perhaps relieved or grateful that her father has someone close by.

grounding: Shows a young adult abroad honouring an elderly neighbour through practical care, time and listening, understood across cultures.

passage:
At the old-age home in Shillong, run by a church trust, nobody touched anyone's feet. It wasn't the custom there. Hrithik, twenty-five, from Varanasi, had grown up doing it for every elder, and in his first week as a care worker he felt strangely empty-handed. How was he supposed to show respect?
His colleague Devika, a local nurse, watched him fuss over it. "You'll see," she said.
So Hrithik did what he could. He learnt each resident's name and story. He sat with Mr Kharkongor every afternoon and listened to the same war stories, asking new questions each time. He brought Mrs Syiem her tea exactly as she liked it, weak, three sugars. When old Mr Lyngdoh couldn't sleep, Hrithik read to him. A month later, Mrs Syiem told Devika, "That boy respects us more than my own grandsons." Hrithik heard it from the corridor, and smiled.

qa.q: How does Mrs Syiem like her tea?
qa.a: Weak, with three sugars.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel in his first week at the home?
qa.a: He felt strangely empty-handed and unsure, not knowing how to show respect without touching feet.

qa.q: How did Hrithik show respect without the custom?
qa.a: Through care, time and listening: learning names and stories, sitting with residents, making tea just right and reading to someone who couldn't sleep.

qa.q: How does Mrs Syiem see Hrithik?
qa.a: She sees him as deeply respectful, even more than her own grandsons, because of his attention and care.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who respects elders through care, time and listening where feet-touching is not practised.
